claims.text: Differential thermal contraction during cooling of HfNbTaTiZr generates residual internal stresses through thermal-expansion mismatch.
Thermal-mismatch residual stresses modify dislocation activity and lattice distortion.
A residual-stress mechanism can unify the alloy's elastic-modulus, work-hardening, and high-temperature-creep variations.
The initial HfNbTaTiZr alloy is single-phase BCC.
The initial alloy is polycrystalline and produced by composite solidification.
Standard cooling establishes a nominal residual-stress state in the alloy.
Changing the post-sintering cooling rate systematically changes the magnitude of thermal-mismatch residual stress.
Residual stresses occur at grain boundaries and within the matrix and alter the effective stress field around dislocations.
Residual stress fields created during cooling act as barriers to dislocation motion.
Residual internal stresses enhance the apparent elastic modulus at lower temperatures.
Residual internal stresses increase work hardening by pinning dislocations.
Residual internal stresses modify high-temperature creep by changing the activation-energy landscape for dislocation glide.
Rapid cooling minimizes thermal-expansion mismatch and residual-stress magnitude.
Slow cooling enhances thermal mismatch and produces higher yield strength than rapid cooling.
Slowly cooled samples exhibit higher strain-hardening rates than rapidly cooled samples.
Slowly cooled samples exhibit a lower tensile-creep rate at 1250 °C than rapidly cooled samples.
Cooling-induced residual stresses produce measurable shifts in elastic modulus.
The proposed unifying mechanism applies from 293 to 1250 K and during aging at 600–800 °C.
Precipitation, segregation, or phase changes may introduce effects in addition to residual-stress strengthening.
Rapidly and slowly cooled samples can retain equivalent phase distributions so that residual stress is the only material-state difference.

contradictions.description: The creep experiment is specified at approximately 1250 °C, equivalent to about 1523 K, while the stated upper boundary of the unified mechanism is 1250 K.

The design assumes cooling rate changes only residual stress while preserving equivalent phase distributions, but the cited same-system evidence states that slower cooling caused BCC1 decomposition whereas rapid cooling preserved the metastable single-phase BCC1 state. Thus the proposed comparison is not demonstrated to isolate residual stress.
